headline: High-risk git/workspace overlap: Aider can write shared repos while mem0 adds no isolation, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and shares state via a shared git repo; mem0 has no documented isolation or provenance controls. That creates a plausible file-based injection path if mem0 stores attacker-controlled text that Aider later ingests. The pathway is not proven by docs, so I rate it medium rather than high.
conditions: IF mem0 writes attacker-controlled text into the shared repo or adjacent workspace
IF Aider later reads that content as instructions or context without provenance checks
mitigations: Store mem0 data outside the shared git repo
Add a manual review step before Aider consumes mem0-generated text
Prefix mem0 outputs with a non-executable delimiter
Use separate OS users or containers for the two agents
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and filtering before ingestion

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history and can write files in a shared repo; mem0 is a knowledge-management agent with no stated data-class limits or isolation. If mem0 persists or re-emits repo content, sensitive code or history can leak across the pair. The profiles do not show direct exfiltration by mem0, so medium is the safest choice.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or git history is stored in mem0 memory
IF mem0 later surfaces that memory to another consumer or UI
mitigations: Exclude secrets and private code from mem0 ingestion
Limit mem0 to metadata-only entries
Rotate or redact sensitive repo history before syncing
Review mem0 retention settings before use
requires-engineering: enforce per-data-class access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider has unrestricted filesystem write and modify_git_state, and its concurrency model explicitly shares state via a shared git repo. mem0 has no documented locking or coordination primitives. Concurrent writes to the same repo can clobber commits or corrupt state, and the default Aider workflow is already git-mutating, so this is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or working tree
IF mem0 or another wrapper mutates files that Aider also edits
mitigations: Run the agents in separate working trees
Serialize writes with a simple lock file
Disable concurrent edits during Aider commit operations
Use branch-per-agent workflows
requires-engineering: add transactional merge/lock coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can produce code changes and git commits, while mem0 is a memory system that may treat stored text as authoritative context. If mem0 feeds Aider output back without verification, errors can cascade into repeated bad edits. The profiles do not show autonomous downstream actions beyond repo edits, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF mem0 stores Aider-generated claims as trusted memory
IF later prompts to Aider reuse that memory without human verification
mitigations: Require human review before reusing stored memory
Keep a source-of-truth note separate from agent memory
Tag Aider outputs as unverified until checked
Clear stale memory entries after each task
requires-engineering: add confidence scoring and citation checks

E_compliance.rationale: Aider explicitly handles source code, git history, and provider API keys, while mem0 has no documented residency, retention, or certification claims in the profile. The main issue is a documentation gap rather than a proven mismatch, so low is appropriate. I cite only Aider because the compliance concern is driven by its handled data classes and the absence of matching controls in mem0.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are stored in the shared workflow
IF mem0 retains data longer than the operator expects
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in the shared repo
Review mem0 retention and deletion settings
Keep API keys out of agent-visible files
Document a data-handling policy for the pair
requires-engineering: obtain vendor compliance attestations
